## What to read
notes/easel_guide.md; notes/studio_notes.md;
notes/research/friedrich_materials.md (his materials and method, sourced);
notes/research/trees.md (how trees are built) and
notes/research/oil_paint_physics.md as needed.

## Working
- You make every artistic decision.
- Friedrich's pictures are full of small, particular details; don't stop at broad
  passages.
- Look at your painting often, whole and close up.
- Keep a working journal with `bin/easel note "..."` as you go: your own
  working notes. Add to it; don't rewrite earlier entries.
- Develop the painting until you judge it complete. Then save it
  (`bin/easel save`) and close the session.

## When you're done
Reply with the paths of the saved painting and its log, the painting's
title if you give it one, and if you like a few sentences about the
picture.

` is 3, `7 / 2` is
  3.5). Bitwise operators are built in; there is no `unpack` (use
  `table.unpack`). Loop variables are read-only. Don't write `global`
  declarations (one switches its chunk to strict mode).
- **`pairs` walks a table in the same order in every session and replay.**
  Tables keyed by strings, numbers and booleans walk in Lua's order; a
  table with any other key walks in a fixed order (booleans, numbers,
  strings, then other keys in the order they were made). For a big list,
  `ipairs` is faster.
- **Memory.** A mask costs 4 bytes a pixel, a form 28. Keep big things
  `local` when later chunks don't need them.

## The journal

`notes/journal.md` is your working journal. `bin/easel note '<text>'` (or
`bin/easel note -` to read the text from stdin) appends an entry stamped
with the session's painting time, such as `day 2, 09:40`; the session must
be open. Entries already there stay as they were written; writing a note
doesn't advance painting time.

## The log

`bin/easel check` replays the log in a fresh session and compares it with
the live canvas. The log, `paintings/lua/painting.lua`, is plain Lua with
a line `--@ chunk N` before each chunk. The easel keeps a record of it in
`out/easel/painting/committed.lua`. If the log is changed, shortened or
missing, the easel refuses to continue.

at 30 and 50 hours, and dry in places by 98. A lead-white patch was still tacky at 3 days and dry at 5.
- A dark passage with bone black was still tacky 5 days after it was laid.

## Masks and edges
- A noise mask scaled for perspective turned too fine toward the far band and read as camouflage.
- A mask helper with a slope error put a pass in the wrong place, so the pass barely changed anything. An explicit `below()` curve fixed it.
- A keep-out mask built from the shapes in front and subtracted from each later pass protected them.
## Brushes
- A 2H pencil at pressure 0.2–0.3 barely showed in the whole view and needed a crop to see.
- A pale-loaded rigger 0.9 over a pale field laid stick-thin lines too faint to read.
- A rigger 1.1, with two strokes ramped in pressure from 0.1 to 0.55 and back, made small V marks.
- An unclipped thick vertical stroke overshot onto a neighboring shape and left a dark streak.
## Looking and the session
- Crops over 1200 px (500 units) are refused. A grid crop helped with placing coordinates, and `--mode value` and `squint` helped judge the whole.

events.text:
The journal's empty, so I'll think about composition ideas instead — something in Friedrich's style for a June scene, like meadows near Greifswald with a distant town silhouette, church spires, and windmills against a wide flat landscape.

I'm settling on a wide June meadow near the Baltic coast: low horizon, distant town silhouette with spires and a windmill, a solitary oak, two Rückenfigur figures on a path, sky taking two-thirds of the frame with a warm-to-blue gradient and fine cloud streaks, plus sheep, a fence, a hay wagon, and a small sailboat on a lagoon. I'll set the canvas at roughly 1000x700 with the horizon around two-thirds up, titling it something like "June Morning on the Bodden Meadows," and start laying out the composition coordinates.

Now I'm mapping out the details layer by layer: a distant strip of Bodden water glinting near the horizon, a town silhouette with three distinct church towers plus rooftops fading into bluish haze, a small windmill off to the left, and a curving path through meadow greens that darken and warm toward the foreground, with a row of pollard willows and grazing horses in the middle distance, leading into a foreground strip of individual grass stalks and flowers.

I'm adding two small figures walking away toward town along the path, plus a fence post and buttercups for seasonal detail, then noting the pigment palette (lead white, smalt, cobalt, ochres, vermilion, Prussian blue, green earth) and the underpainting sequence — a warm red-earth ground layer knifed in first, then a lighter lead-white-and-ochre layer brushed or rolled over it.

Now I'm sketching the process: pencil underdrawing of the horizon, town silhouette, windmill, willow row, path, and figures, followed by a very thin Friedrich-style imprimatura on the land. For the sky, I'm working out how to build graded horizontal bands using smoothstep masks and overlapping passes so the color transitions from warm near the horizon to cobalt at the top without harsh stripes, possibly using threshold-based coverage or stippling to soften the banding.

I'm settling on stippling the sky with graded coverage functions—laying a broad mid-tone base with horizontal hatching, then stippling lighter tones near the horizon and darker blue toward the top with coverage that increases in each direction, blending while wet with clipped horizontal passes. I want to experiment with this technique and see how it looks before committing, so I'm setting up a scratch directory to start testing.

I realize it's now 16:03 — six hours have passed, and the lead white has likely gelled by now, so blending won't be effective anymore since the paint is setting. The better strategy is to let this base dry completely, then apply a second full sky layer in thin, graded coats to achieve a smoother gradient, following Friedrich's approach of building up thin layers.

I'm also reconsidering the horizon color — it's reading too yellow-beige, like ground rather than a pale June sky. I need to redefine the gradient into eight bands from top to horizon, shifting the mix toward more white and pale smalt with just a touch of ochre and vermilion near the bottom for warmth, rather than the current heavier ochre tones. This second layer will have to wait a couple days for the base to fully dry first.

I'm also thinking through timing: painting the whole sky at coverage 1.6 takes about 80 minutes, so I need to work top-down in overlapping chunks and blend each region right after painting it, before the lead-white starts to gel, using overlapping blend zones to avoid visible seams between segments.

For thinner films this time, I'll drop the medium to 0.15 and use a lighter load, letting the dry base show through slightly since the new layer's 0.82 hiding power still mostly covers the underlying steps — then wait two days before continuing.

Since new strokes sit on top on tacky paint, darks work fine layered now — so I'll move to reworking the crown brooms since they're dry. For each willow I'm fanning rods out from the head point at varying angles and lengths, using a hatch pattern clipped to a broom-shaped mask.

Actually rethinking the crown shape — instead of the current roughly circular ball, a pollard's crown is more like an inverted cone: narrow near the head and broadening upward into a domed top, closer to how these trees actually look in full June leaf. The tricky part is that the new mask won't fully cover the old circular crown, so I'd need to paint over the exposed lower sides with meadow color to blend it in cleanly.

Rather than reshaping the whole silhouette, I think the fix is subtler: keep the rounded head but break up the too-regular "broccoli" stippled texture by adding thin rods fanning out from the top and sides with leaves, making the outline feathery and taller, with darker gaps breaking up the lumpiness. I'll add silvery-green rigger strokes fanning from the head, extending past the outline by about 8*s, to give it that broom-like character.

**Title:** *June Morning on the Meadows by the Ryck*

It's an invented Pomeranian coastal landscape. The horizon is low, so the sky takes up two thirds of the canvas, shading from smalt blue at the top to a warm, pale haze with a bank of cumulus low on the left. A man in a dark greatcoat and a woman in a red-brown dress with a cream shawl stand on a worn footpath with their backs to us. They look over the June grass, across a thin silver channel of river, to a small town: a baroque-capped tower, a squat tower, a slender spire and long church roofs, all in blue-grey. A row of pollard willows holds the left side, with a post mill showing between them. On the right a split-rail fence runs back toward the water, with a bay and a black horse in the pasture beyond it and a red sail far off. The small things are painted in the foreground: buttercups, daisies, sorrel, seed heads and cow parsley, plus birds and belfry openings in the distance.

The sky took a second layer of eight graded bands to lose its stepped bands. I painted out the first willow row and redrew it at full size after measuring the figures against the eye height showed it was the size of shrubs, and I moved the horses farther back for the same reason. I also learned, more than once, not to blend next to fresh dark paint.

`io`, `os`, `debug`, `require`, `dofile`, `loadfile`

- **Lua 5.5.** Numbers are integers or floats (`7 // 2` is 3, `7 / 2` is
  3.5). Bitwise operators are built in; there is no `unpack` (use
  `table.unpack`). Loop variables are read-only. Don't write `global`
  declarations (one switches its chunk to strict mode).
- **`pairs` walks a table in the same order in every session and replay.**
  Tables keyed by strings, numbers and booleans walk in Lua's order; a
  table with any other key walks in a fixed order (booleans, numbers,
  strings, then other keys in the order they were made). For a big list,
  `ipairs` is faster.
- **Memory.** A mask costs 4 bytes a pixel, a form 28. Keep big things
  `local` when later chunks don't need them.

## The journal

`notes/journal.md` is your working journal. `bin/easel note '<text>'` (or
`bin/easel note -` to read the text from stdin) appends an entry stamped
with the session's painting time, such as `day 2, 09:40`; the session must
be open. Entries already there stay as they were written; writing a note
doesn't advance painting time.

## The log

`bin/easel check` replays the log in a fresh session and compares it with
the live canvas. The log, `paintings/lua/painting.lua`, is plain Lua with
a line `--@ chunk N` before each chunk. The easel keeps a record of it in
`out/easel/painting/committed.lua`. If the log is changed, shortened or
missing, the easel refuses to continue.

- **Title:** *Morning on the Ryck Meadows*

It's a June forenoon on the flat meadows outside a small Pomeranian town, invented in Friedrich's way. The horizon is set low, so a pale, hazy sky takes up two thirds of the canvas. A man in a dark greatcoat and a woman in a red-brown dress and cream shawl stand on a worn path, their backs to us. They look across the meadow and a thin stretch of the river Ryck to the grey-blue towers of the town, which has a skirt of low houses and trees. On the left a row of pollard willows (trees cut back to a stump so shoots grow from the top) holds the edge of the picture, and a post mill on the rise shows between them. On the right a split-rail fence runs down to the river. A bay grazes behind it and a black horse stands. A red sail sits on the water in the distance. The foreground has buttercups, daisies, sorrel and cow parsley.

When I came back to the easel, my last session had called the picture done but hadn't saved it. I made two final changes before saving:
- **The horses:** the black horse got a cool sheen of sky light along its crest, back and rump, and the bay a warm lit back, so they no longer read as flat cut-outs.
- **A stork:** I added a white stork walking between the first two willows, with a black wing and red legs and bill, its feet in the grass.

Both were small enough to do safely on paint that was already dry.

I didn't run `bin/easel check` to replay the log against the canvas. It took about 13 minutes at 208 chunks, and this log is now 189 chunks.

`io`, `os`, `debug`, `require`, `dofile`, `loadfile`
  and `collectgarbage` aren't there. `print` goes to the reply.
- **Lua 5.5.** Numbers are integers or floats (`7 // 2` is 3, `7 / 2` is
  3.5). Bitwise operators are built in; there is no `unpack` (use
  `table.unpack`). Loop variables are read-only. Don't write `global`
  declarations (one switches its chunk to strict mode).
- **`pairs` walks a table in the same order in every session and replay.**
  Tables keyed by strings, numbers and booleans walk in Lua's order; a
  table with any other key walks in a fixed order (booleans, numbers,
  strings, then other keys in the order they were made). For a big list,
  `ipairs` is faster.
- **Memory.** A mask costs 4 bytes a pixel, a form 28. Keep big things
  `local` when later chunks don't need them.

## The journal

`notes/journal.md` is your working journal. `bin/easel note '<text>'` (or
`bin/easel note -` to read the text from stdin) appends an entry stamped
with the session's painting time, such as `day 2, 09:40`; the session must
be open. Entries already there stay as they were written; writing a note
doesn't advance painting time.

## The log

`bin/easel check` replays the log in a fresh session and compares it with
the live canvas. The log, `paintings/lua/painting.lua`, is plain Lua with
a line `--@ chunk N` before each chunk. The easel keeps a record of it in
`out/easel/painting/committed.lua`. If the log is changed, shortened or
missing, the easel refuses to continue.

Since the light hits the man's figure from the left, I'm adding a dark center back vent line and a lighter ridge along the shoulder blade, plus a half-belt detail at the waist with two tiny buttons — a period-accurate greatcoat feature. Below the waist I'm placing two faint lighter fold lines to suggest the coat's drape.

For the woman's dress, I'm painting dark fold lines spreading from the waist down to the hem with a lit ridge between them, and adding shawl shading that converges to a point near the waist. I'll keep using a small round brush with light, single strokes, working from the existing color piles I've built up for the coat, dress, and shawl.

- **Title:** *Morning on the Ryck Meadows*

It's a June forenoon on the flat meadows by the Bodden, outside a small Pomeranian town. The town is my own invention. The horizon sits low, so the pale summer sky takes up about two thirds of the canvas. Two figures stand on a worn path, seen from behind in Friedrich's way: a man in a dark greatcoat and a woman in a red-brown dress with a cream shawl. They look across the meadows to the town, a grey-blue silhouette of towers and a spire with low houses and trees at their foot. On the left a row of pollard willows gives a dark frame, with a post mill on the rise showing through a gap and a stork hunting in the grass. On the right a split-rail fence runs back towards the river, with a grazing bay horse and a black horse behind it. The foreground is full of small things: tall grass stems, seed heads, buttercups, daisies, sorrel and clover, with cow parsley in both lower corners.

In this last short sitting I only did small work on the figures. The man's coat got a half-belt with two buttons, a back vent and a few lit folds. The woman's dress got folds falling from the waist, and her shawl two soft folds running to its point. I left the pale mark around the black horse's head because it reads as a halter.

The easel's replay check didn't run a full comparison this time: it reported the log intact and put off the final verification until delivery.
